connection: Begin in the empty learner workspace. No solution, projects, production code, tests, or experiments exist yet. Scaffold the permanent TimeClock production, test, and ScratchPad projects in the learner workspace.
objectives: Explain what a solution (.sln) is and what a project (.csproj) is, and how the two relate.
Distinguish a console application, a class library, an ASP.NET Core web project, and an xUnit test project by what each one produces.
Use dotnet new to generate a solution and all six permanent projects.
Explain why source projects live under src/ and test projects live under tests/.
Use dotnet sln add and dotnet build to assemble and build a solution from independently created projects.
Choose project folders by architectural responsibility and explain when each one should be added.
Explain why an empty folder disappears from a fresh git clone, and how a .gitkeep file prevents that.

visuals.title: A solution is a list of projects, not a project itself
visuals.explanation: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln does not contain code. It is a manifest that names which .csproj files belong together so one command can build or test all of them.

visuals.title: dotnet new turns a template name into a folder
visuals.explanation: dotnet new classlib -o src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain creates a folder containing PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.csproj and a starter .cs file. The -o path is also where the project will live.

visuals.title: A test project is a project, with one extra job
visuals.explanation: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests is an ordinary class library plus the xUnit package. Nothing about its .csproj is structurally special — only its purpose is.

visuals.title: A folder with nothing tracked inside it does not survive a clone
visuals.explanation: Git records files, not directories. An empty Validators/ folder exists on your disk but vanishes the moment someone clones the repository, unless a file — even an empty .gitkeep — lives inside it.

options: Compiled C# code for the whole application
A list of project paths and build configurations, no source code
preQuiz.explanation: A .sln file is a manifest. The code lives entirely inside the .csproj-owning folders it lists.

preQuiz.prompt: What is the structural difference between a console application project and a class library project, right after dotnet new creates each one?
options: A console app's .csproj sets OutputType to Exe and has an entry point; a class library has neither
Class libraries cannot contain any methods
xUnit test projects are console applications internally
preQuiz.explanation: A console app is built to run directly (an .exe with a Main entry point); a class library is built to be referenced by something else and has no entry point of its own.

preQuiz.prompt: You run dotnet new classlib -o src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain but never run dotnet sln add. What happens when you later run dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln?
options: The new project builds along with the others automatically because it's in a src/ folder
The new project is silently skipped — the solution only builds what it's told to include
dotnet build fails immediately because the folder isn't registered
preQuiz.explanation: Folder presence is not membership. A project only participates in solution-wide build/test/restore once it's listed inside the .sln file.

concept.title: A solution groups projects; a project is the buildable unit
paragraphs: A .csproj file is the actual unit the .NET toolchain compiles: it lists a target framework, its dependencies, and the source files that belong to it. Every meaningful thing — building, running, testing, publishing — ultimately happens at the level of one .csproj.

A .sln file is a manifest of project paths. By the end of this lab it lists Domain, App, Infrastructure, Web, ScratchPad, and Domain.Tests so one build or test command can act on the complete learner workspace.

concept.title: Four templates, six permanent projects
paragraphs: dotnet new console creates a runnable project. App is the production console host; ScratchPad is a second console project used only as the permanent learning notebook.
dotnet new classlib creates Domain and Infrastructure because neither runs by itself. dotnet new web creates the HTTP host. dotnet new xunit creates the permanent test project.
The lab creates all six projects. ScratchPad is never deleted, and production projects never reference it.

concept.title: src/ and tests/ are convention, not a compiler rule
paragraphs: src/ and tests/ are ordinary folders used only to organize the repository. Neither name has special meaning to .NET or the compiler: src/ contains one or more source projects, tests/ contains one or more test projects, and each .csproj project — not either folder — is an actual buildable unit.

A small solution may have one test project, such as PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests. Larger professional solutions commonly have several, such as Domain.Tests, Infrastructure.Tests, Web.Tests, and Integration.Tests, all organized under tests/.

The mental model is: the solution lists projects; src/ holds source projects; tests/ holds test projects; and projects are what build. Creating these items is separate too — dotnet new creates the solution or project files, while dotnet sln add registers a project in the solution without moving its source code. The lab provides the complete copyable command sequence.

concept.title: Folder map: which folders belong inside each project folder
paragraphs: Each dotnet new command creates a project folder containing a .csproj file. The src/ folder contains the five source project folders. The tests/ folder contains the test project folder.

A project folder may later contain smaller subfolders that group related C# files. The table names every project folder created in Session 01 and shows which subfolders may belong inside it later. Do not create the optional subfolders now; create each one only when the course adds its first real file.

headers: What belongs in this project folder
rows: Business concepts and business rules that do not depend on databases, terminals, or HTTP.
Usually none at first; application Services/ only if coordination grows
Program startup, dependency wiring, and console workflow coordination.
Concrete storage and persistence code that is allowed to know about database technology.
Requests/, Responses/, Validators/, Mappings/, Configuration/, Options/
HTTP endpoints and the input, output, validation, mapping, and configuration files used at the web boundary.
Permanent learning experiments. Production projects must not depend on this project folder.
None required at first; organize test folders only when the suite grows
Test files that verify Domain behavior. This project folder belongs under tests/, not src/.

closingParagraphs: The word Services does not identify one automatic folder location. A domain service folder contains business rules and belongs inside the Domain project folder. An application service folder coordinates a workflow and may belong inside the App project folder or a later Application project folder.

Interfaces/, Constants/, Extensions/, and Helpers/ are also not automatic folders. Place a file in the project folder that owns its responsibility, and add a subfolder only when multiple related files make that grouping useful.

concept.title: Git tracks files, not empty folders
paragraphs: Git's index stores blobs (file contents) and trees (directory listings that point at blobs), never a directory entry with nothing inside it. An empty Validators/ folder can sit on your disk for weeks, but the moment you git add . and commit, nothing gets recorded for it — there's no file to point at. Clone the repository fresh, or check out that commit somewhere else, and Validators/ simply isn't there.

If an empty folder genuinely must exist before its contents, the smallest tracked placeholder is an empty .gitkeep. Git gives that filename no special behavior; it is only a recognizable community convention. A short README.md can document the folder instead. Most of the time, the better choice is to wait and create the folder with its first real file.

Session 01 does not need placeholder folders because it creates only the projects. If a later change deliberately adds an empty folder before its first source file, a .gitkeep can preserve it—but creating the real file and folder together is usually clearer.

lab.objective: Scaffold the permanent TimeClock production, test, and ScratchPad projects in the learner workspace.
lab.startingCondition: Begin in the empty learner workspace. No solution, projects, production code, tests, or experiments exist yet.

steps.text: In a Bash-compatible terminal, define names for the solution file and all six project folders. These are temporary terminal variables, not C# variables. For now, notice that name=value stores text and $name reuses it; C# variables are taught properly in Session 03. Keep this terminal open for the remaining steps.
Create the classic solution file using solution_name. Quoting the variable keeps the command safe if a future name contains spaces.

Create the four production projects, the permanent ScratchPad console project, and the Domain test project using the folder variables. ScratchPad is a notebook that stays in the solution for the entire course.
steps.code:
dotnet new classlib -o "$domain_project"
dotnet new console -o "$app_project"
dotnet new classlib -o "$infrastructure_project"
dotnet new web -o "$web_project"
dotnet new console -o "$scratchpad_project"
dotnet new xunit -o "$domain_tests_project"

steps.text: Add all six projects to solution_file. Each project path reuses both its folder variable and solution_name. Creating a project does not add it automatically.
steps.code:
dotnet sln "$solution_file" add "$domain_project/${solution_name}.Domain.csproj"
dotnet sln "$solution_file" add "$app_project/${solution_name}.App.csproj"
dotnet sln "$solution_file" add "$infrastructure_project/${solution_name}.Infrastructure.csproj"
dotnet sln "$solution_file" add "$web_project/${solution_name}.Web.csproj"
dotnet sln "$solution_file" add "$scratchpad_project/${solution_name}.ScratchPad.csproj"
dotnet sln "$solution_file" add "$domain_tests_project/${solution_name}.Domain.Tests.csproj"

steps.text: List and build solution_file. Expect six project paths and zero build errors.

lab.expectedBehavior: One persistent learner solution contains four production projects, one ScratchPad project, and one test project. It builds before any business code is added.
lab.validation:
solution_file="PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln"
dotnet build "$solution_file" --configuration Release && dotnet test "$solution_file" --configuration Release --no-build

Record the infrastructure template until EF persistence replaces it.

Keep the lesson synchronized with the cumulative build step.

review: The lab uses solution because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.

postQuiz.prompt: You run dotnet new console -o src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App but never run dotnet sln add. Later, dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln succeeds with no mention of PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App. Why?
options: Console apps build automatically once created
PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App was never added to the solution, so the solution build has no reason to know it exists
dotnet build always finds every .csproj under the current directory
postQuiz.explanation: A folder on disk and a solution member are two different things. Only dotnet sln add creates the membership dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln relies on.

postQuiz.prompt: You create mkdir -p src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/Validators, write no files into it, and commit. A teammate clones the repository fresh. What do they see?
options: An empty Validators/ folder, exactly as you left it
No Validators/ folder at all, because git never recorded an empty directory
A build error, because the folder is referenced somewhere
postQuiz.explanation: Git's index only tracks files (and the directory structure implied by their paths). A directory with nothing tracked inside it is invisible to git add and disappears on clone.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does Repositories/ belong under PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure rather than PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain, even though the repository interfaces (Interfaces/) live in Domain?
options: Infrastructure is just an arbitrary place to put extra folders
Domain should not depend on any specific storage technology, so the concrete, storage-aware implementations live in the project that's allowed to know about EF Core
Interfaces and their implementations must always be in different solutions
postQuiz.explanation: Keeping concrete repository implementations out of Domain is what lets Domain stay reusable by any consumer, regardless of what storage technology that consumer eventually chooses.

reflections: Which command created files on disk, and which command changed what dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln considers in scope?
Choose one folder from the responsibility table. Which TimeClock project would own it, and what real code would justify creating it?
Why does an empty .gitkeep file count as a legitimate fix for git's empty-directory problem instead of a hack, given that git itself gives the filename no special meaning at all?
whatBreaks: Skipping dotnet sln add leaves a project that builds standalone but is invisible to solution-wide build/test/restore commands. An intentionally empty folder without a tracked file silently vanishes for every teammate who clones the repository. Putting Repositories/ or other storage-aware code inside PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain would make Domain depend on a specific storage technology, undermining the reusability the next session builds on.
summary: A solution is a manifest naming which projects build and test together; a project is the actual buildable unit. As TimeClock grows, folders are added for real code according to project responsibility—not from a mandatory universal checklist. Domain owns business rules, Infrastructure owns persistence details, Web owns HTTP boundaries, and host or application code coordinates use cases. Situational folders belong wherever their contents are owned.
